title: SELF JOIN
description: Learn how to use the SELF JOIN to join a table to itself for querying hierarchical data or comparing rows within the same table.

data.text: A self join allows you to join a table to itself. It helps you query hierarchical data or compare rows within the same table.

A self join uses the INNER JOIN or LEFT JOIN clause. Because the query that uses a self join references the same table, a table alias is used to assign different names to the same table within the query.

data.title: Important
data.text: Referencing the same table more than once in a query without using table aliases will result in an error.

data.title: SELF JOIN Syntax
data.content: Join table T to itself using aliases t1 and t2.
data.code:
SELECT
    select_list
FROM
    T t1
[INNER | LEFT] JOIN T t2 ON
    join_predicate;

data.text: The query references the table T twice. The table aliases t1 and t2 are used to assign different names to the T table in the query.

Consider the staffs table from the sample database. The staffs table stores staff information such as id, first name, last name, and email. It also has a column named manager_id that specifies the direct manager. For example, an employee reports to their manager because the manager_id value of the employee matches the staff_id of the manager. The top-level manager has no manager, so the manager_id column has a NULL value.

data.title: Self Join with INNER JOIN
data.content: Use table aliases e for employees and m for managers to show who reports to whom.
data.code:
SELECT
    e.first_name + ' ' + e.last_name employee,
    m.first_name + ' ' + m.last_name manager
FROM
    sales.staffs e
INNER JOIN sales.staffs m ON m.staff_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY
    manager;

data.text: In this example, we referenced the staffs table twice: once as e for employees and again as m for managers. The join predicate matches the employee and manager relationship using the values in the e.manager_id and m.staff_id columns.
The employee column does not include the top-level manager because of the INNER JOIN effect. If you replace the INNER JOIN with a LEFT JOIN, the result set will include the top-level manager.

data.title: Self Join with LEFT JOIN
data.content: LEFT JOIN includes employees who have no manager.
data.code:
SELECT
    e.first_name + ' ' + e.last_name employee,
    m.first_name + ' ' + m.last_name manager
FROM
    sales.staffs e
LEFT JOIN sales.staffs m ON m.staff_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY
    manager;

data.text: Self Join to Compare Rows in the Same Table

data.title: Find Customers in the Same City (with >)
data.content: The condition c1.customer_id > c2.customer_id prevents comparing the same customer.
data.code:
SELECT
    c1.city,
    c1.first_name + ' ' + c1.last_name customer_1,
    c2.first_name + ' ' + c2.last_name customer_2
FROM
    sales.customers c1
INNER JOIN sales.customers c2 ON c1.customer_id > c2.customer_id
AND c1.city = c2.city
ORDER BY
    city,
    customer_1,
    customer_2;

data.text: The condition c1.customer_id > c2.customer_id ensures that the statement does not compare the same customer. The condition c1.city = c2.city matches the city of the two customers.
If you change the greater than (>) operator to the not equal to (<>) operator, you will get more rows because every non-matching pairing is included.

data.title: Comparison Operators in Self Joins
data.text: The > operator in the ON clause prevents duplicate comparisons. The <> operator includes all pairs of different customers, resulting in more rows.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: A self join joins a table to itself using INNER JOIN or LEFT JOIN.
Table aliases are required when referencing the same table multiple times.
Self joins are useful for querying hierarchical data and comparing rows within the same table.
Use the > operator in the ON clause to avoid duplicate comparisons.
LEFT JOIN in a self join includes rows with no match (e.g., top-level managers).
